title: The salok of wonder
hookLine: wonder is the sound, wonder the scripture, wonder the creatures, wonder the colors (Asa di Var, ang 463)

cards: Watch a toddler meet a dog for the first time. The eyes go wide. The mouth opens.

Sometimes there's a long whoa, sometimes just a small body gone still with astonishment. Then the child points and looks at you: are you seeing this? Somewhere along the way, grown-ups stop making that face.
We've seen dogs. We've seen rain. Guru Nanak, in Asa di Var, writes a salok that sounds like that toddler's whoa, over and over.

teach.b: The salok begins almost every phrase with one word: vismaad. Wonder, awe, astonishment. In paraphrase, it runs like this.
Wonder is the sound, wonder is the sacred knowledge. Wonder are the living beings, wonder their many kinds. Wonder are the forms, wonder the colors.
Wonder is the wind, wonder the water, wonder the fire that plays its marvels. Wonder the earth, wonder the sources of life. Wonder, union; wonder, parting.
Wonder, hunger; wonder, being fed. Wonder near, wonder far. It keeps going, line after line, like a drumbeat.
Notice what Guru Nanak puts on the list. Not only lovely things.

teach.h: HUNGER AND PARTING ARE ON THE LIST.
teach.b: Parting is there, and hunger, and the wilderness alongside the path. Vismaad isn't a sunset filter laid over the hard parts of life. It's astonishment at all of it, the strange, enormous fact that anything exists at all.
Then the ending, in paraphrase: seeing these marvels, I am struck with wonder. Nanak says, to understand this comes by perfect good fortune. In Sikh teaching, vismaad is more than a feeling.
It's a spiritual state: the place where cleverness runs out and only awe is left.
Sikh tradition hears the same awe in the name Waheguru, which opens with waah, the Punjabi cry of wonder.
The toddler's whoa is not so far from prayer.

how: Asa di Var's salok of wonder, sung each morning in gurdwaras, repeats vismaad line after line, and Sikhs hear the same awe in waah, the opening of Waheguru.

o: fear of a stern, distant God
a sad longing for what is gone

p: the cry of wonder in Waheguru
on the list of wonders too

s: the salok of wonder lists only beautiful things
hunger, parting and the wilderness are on the list too.
vismaad begins almost every phrase of the salok
line after line, like a drumbeat.
in Sikh teaching vismaad is only a passing mood
it's a spiritual state, where cleverness runs out and awe is left.

games.q: Guru Nanak looks at the whole of creation, hunger and parting included. what does the salok say he feels?
o: wonder: seeing these marvels, I am struck with wonder.
games.why: vismaad. the salok ends: seeing these marvels, I am wonderstruck; understanding this comes by perfect good fortune.

practice: Look out a window, or picture the last time you were outdoors, and wait until something catches you: a cloud, a weed in a crack, a bird. Stay with it and let it be astonishing, then find a second wonder, and a third.
If you pray, whisper Waheguru at each one.

wordCard.voice: Vismaad. Wonder and awe; Guru Nanak's salok in Asa di Var sees vismaad in sound, beings, colors, wind, water, hunger and parting, near and far.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vismaad, wonder or awe; Guru Nanak repeats it through a whole salok.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder, wonder. Grown-ups are allowed to say whoa. That's day five hundred forty-one.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok Mahala 1 (vismaad naad), Guru Nanak (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463–464)
